## From Terminal to Desktop

The backend for NoteSearch was complete — a working inverted index, keyword
search, scoring, and snippet extraction, all in pure C++. But it lived behind
a terminal loop. For a tool I actually want to use every day, that isn't good
enough. This phase was about wrapping that engine in a proper desktop application
using Qt Widgets.

The guiding principle throughout was clean separation: the backend knows nothing
about Qt, and Qt knows nothing about the indexing logic. The UI is a shell that
passes user input in and displays results out. Nothing more.

## Why Qt

For a personal desktop tool that lives entirely offline with no web dependencies,
the realistic C++ UI options are Qt, wxWidgets, and Dear ImGui. Qt stood out for
two reasons. First, it produces genuinely professional-looking native applications
on Windows without much effort. Second, Qt is widely used in industry; embedded
systems, desktop software, internal tooling makes for a great learning opportunity.
The cross platform nature of Qt is a bonus, but Windows is the primary target for this project.

The version used here is Qt 6 with MinGW on Windows, built and managed through
Qt Creator and CMake.

## Architecture: The Shell Pattern

The most important decision in this phase wasn't about UI design — it was about
where the boundary between Qt and C++ sits. The rule I set was strict:

- `Indexer`, `SearchEngine`, and `Tokenizer` are pure C++ with no Qt includes
- `MainWindow` is the only place Qt lives, and it only calls into the backend
  through standard C++ interfaces using `std::string` and `std::vector`

This means the backend could be dropped into any other frontend — a CLI, a
different GUI framework, or a web server — without touching a single line of
indexing or search logic. Qt is genuinely just a shell.

The data flow is straightforward:

```
User action in Qt UI
    → MainWindow converts Qt types to std::string
        → Indexer / SearchEngine does its work
            → Results returned as std::vector
                → MainWindow converts back to Qt types for display
```

The conversion points are small and explicit. `QString::toStdString()` going in,
`QString::fromStdString()` coming out. That's the entire surface area between
the two worlds.

## What the UI Does

The interface is intentionally minimal. There are three interactive elements:

- A directory input and Browse button that opens a native folder picker and
  triggers index building
- A search input and Search button (also triggered by pressing Enter) that runs
  a query against the built index
- A results list that shows each matching file with its relevance score and a
  snippet preview

When a directory is selected, the index builds immediately and the results area
confirms how many unique terms were found. Searches from that point are fast
since the index is already in memory.

## Keeping the Build Clean

Integrating Qt into an existing C++ project required updating the CMake
configuration to declare Qt dependencies and tell the compiler where to find
the backend headers:

```cmake
find_package(Qt6 6.5 REQUIRED COMPONENTS Core Widgets)

target_include_directories(SearchEngine PRIVATE
    ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/include
    ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/src
)
```

The `include/` directory holds the backend headers and `src/` holds all source
files. Keeping them separate makes it visually clear which code belongs to the
engine and which belongs to the UI.

## Reflection

The separation of concerns principle paid off immediately during integration.
Because the backend had no Qt dependencies, dropping it into the Qt project was
straightforward — update CMake, include the headers in `MainWindow`, and call
the same functions that were already working in the terminal version. There was
no refactoring of backend logic at all.

The Qt learning curve was real but manageable. Qt Creator's UI designer makes
laying out widgets intuitive, and Qt's signal and slot system for connecting
button clicks to handler functions is clean once the mental model clicks. The
trickiest part was getting CMake and Qt Creator to agree on where the source
files lived, particularly after reorganizing the project into `src/` and
`include/` subdirectories.

## What's Next

The next phase is extending the indexer to support `.pdf` and `.docx` files,
keeping the same architecture — pure C++ parsers in the backend, no Qt involved
in the parsing logic. The UI will surface file type information in the results
list once that support is in place.
